claims.claim: SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium due to desperation.
Real rent burden worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income under the 2021 ordinance.
The 2021 ordinance capped increases within tenancies but not initial rent levels.
First-generation rent controls (hard caps on levels) consistently cause supply contraction.
Second-generation rent controls (caps on increases) have small or null effects on supply.
The 2021 ordinance is second-generation, explaining stock growth from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
The estimated elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rent levels is 0.31–0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced reduction removes 3–5 percent of stock over five years.
A modelled 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about HK$900 per month to incumbents.
A 15 percent cut leaves 3,000–4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment.
Berlin's Mietendeckel shows caps protect incumbents while the bill goes to those outside.
When the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend.
A hard cap framed as deprivation of income stream would likely attract compensation claims under the Basic Law.
A band-based instrument requires survey infrastructure that does not exist.
A certifiable tenancy register would cost 40–60 staff-years.
Current inspection covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail—tenants with no written agreement.
61 percent of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure.
74 percent of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for a faster public-housing offer.
The better package is tenure security plus a light, indexed band on initial rents.

Mrs Wong's account—nine years, no written agreement, rents set by "whatever the market of desperate newcomers bears" [D4p1]—shows the 2021 instrument left the actual pain point untouched, since it capped increases within tenancies but not initial rent levels [D1p3].

The academic literature distinguishes first-generation controls (hard caps on levels), which show consistent supply contraction, from second-generation controls (caps on increases), which show small or null effects [D6p2].
The 2021 ordinance is second-generation, which explains the stock growth from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1][D6p2].
